desc:
In a binary grid a 1 is land and a 0 is water. An island is a maximal group of land cells connected through the four directions.

You may change at most one water cell into land. Return the size of the largest island you can have afterwards. If the grid contains no water, nothing can be changed and the answer is the size of the whole grid.

grid = [[1,1,0],
        [0,0,1],
        [0,1,1]]   -> 6

Turning the centre cell (1,1) into land joins the island of size 2 (top-left) with the island of size 3 (bottom-right): 2 + 3 + 1 = 6.
hints: Trying every water cell and recounting the islands from scratch costs O((R · C)<sup>2</sup>). Can the island sizes be computed once?
Label each island with an id and store its size. A water cell that is flipped joins the islands of its four neighbours.

For each water cell, collect the distinct island ids around it (a set of up to four ids; two neighbours can belong to the same island), and add 1 plus the sizes of those islands. Also consider the case of no flip, which matters when there is no water.
editorial: First flood-fill every island and give it an id; keep size[id] and a label grid. Then look at each water cell: flipping it creates an island made of the new cell and every neighbouring island. Because two neighbours may belong to the same island, take the set of their ids before summing the sizes, otherwise one island would be counted twice.

The answer is the maximum over all water cells of 1 + sum of sizes of distinct neighbouring islands, and also the largest existing island (relevant when there is no water cell, in which case the whole grid is one island). Everything is O(R · C) time and space.
